subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $x = 2$
Mark 2: $x = -2$

subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$ (correct to TWO decimal places):

$$2x^2 - 6x + 1 = 0$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Correct substitution into the correct formula — $x = \dfrac{6 \pm \sqrt{(-6)^2 - 4(2)(1)}}{2(2)}$
Mark 2: $x = 2{,}82$
Mark 3: $x = 0{,}18$

subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$:

$$x^2 - 90 > x$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Standard form — $x^2 - x - 90 > 0$
Mark 2: Critical values — $(x + 9)(x - 10) > 0$, so CV: $x = -9$ or $x = 10$
Marks 3–4 (double mark): $x < -9$ or $x > 10$ (i.e. $(-\infty\,;\,-9)$ or $(10\,;\,\infty)$)

subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$:

$$x - 7\sqrt{x} = -12$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Isolating the root — $x + 12 = 7\sqrt{x}$
Mark 2: Squaring both sides — $(x + 12)^2 = (7\sqrt{x})^2 \Rightarrow x^2 + 24x + 144 = 49x$
Mark 3: Standard form — $x^2 - 25x + 144 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 16)(x - 9) = 0$
Mark 4: Both answers — $x = 16$ or $x = 9$
(Alternatively let $\sqrt{x} = k$: $(\sqrt{x} - 3)(\sqrt{x} - 4) = 0 \Rightarrow \sqrt{x} = 3$ or $\sqrt{x} = 4 \Rightarrow x = 9$ or $x = 16$.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$ and $y$ simultaneously:

$$2x - y = 2$$
$$xy = 4$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: From eq 1 — $y = 2x - 2$
Mark 2: Substitution — $x(2x - 2) = 4$
Mark 3: Standard form — $2x^2 - 2x - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 - x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 2)(x + 1) = 0$
Mark 4: $x$-values — $x = 2$ or $x = -1$
Mark 5: $y$-values — $y = 2$ or $y = -4$

subQuestions.questionText: Show that $2 \cdot 5^n - 5^{n+1} + 5^{n+2}$ is even for all positive integer values of $n$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Exponent law — $2 \cdot 5^n - 5^n \cdot 5^1 + 5^n \cdot 5^2$
Mark 2: Common factor — $= 5^n(2 - 5 + 25) = 5^n(22)$
Mark 3: Answer/explanation — $= 2\big(5^n(11)\big)$, which is even (OR: any integer multiplied by an even number is even)

subQuestions.questionText:
Determine the values of $x$ and $y$ if:

$$\dfrac{3^{y+1}}{32} = \sqrt{96^x}$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $\dfrac{3^{y+1}}{2^5} = (96)^{\frac{x}{2}}$
Mark 2: $3^{y+1} \cdot 2^{-5} = 2^{\frac{5x}{2}} \cdot 3^{\frac{x}{2}}$
Mark 3: Equating powers of $2$ — $-5 = \dfrac{5x}{2} \Rightarrow x = -2$
Mark 4: Equating powers of $3$ — $y + 1 = \dfrac{x}{2} = -1 \Rightarrow y = -2$

subQuestions.questionText:
The first term of a geometric series is $14$ and the $6^{\text{th}}$ term is $448$.

Calculate the value of the constant ratio, $r$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $T_6 = 14r^5 = 448$, so $r^5 = 32$
Mark 2: $r = 2$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the number of consecutive terms that must be added to the first $6$ terms of the series in order to obtain a sum of $114\,674$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution into the correct formula — $S_6 = \dfrac{14(2^6 - 1)}{2 - 1}$
Mark 2: $S_6 = 882$
Mark 3: $114\,674 - 882 = 113\,792 = 896(2^n - 1) \Rightarrow 128 = 2^n$
Mark 4: $n = 7$, so $7$ more terms must be added to the first $6$ terms
(Alternatively $114\,674 = \dfrac{14(2^n - 1)}{2 - 1} \Rightarrow 2^n = 8\,192 \Rightarrow n = 13$; $13 - 6 = 7$ more terms.)

subQuestions.questionText: If the first term of another series is $448$ and the $6^{\text{th}}$ term is $14$, calculate the sum to infinity of the new series.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$ (from $448r^5 = 14$)
Mark 2: Substitution — $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1 - r} = \dfrac{448}{1 - \frac{1}{2}}$
Mark 3: Answer — $S_\infty = 896$

subQuestions.questionText: If $\displaystyle\sum_{p=0}^{k}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}p + \dfrac{1}{6}\right) = 20\dfrac{1}{6}$, determine the value of $k$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: $T_1 = \dfrac{1}{6}$
Mark 2: $d = \dfrac{3}{6} - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$
Mark 3: Substitution — $\dfrac{121}{6} = \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2\left(\tfrac{1}{6}\right) + (n - 1)\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)\right]$
Mark 4: $121 = n^2 \Rightarrow n = 11$
Mark 5: $k = 10$ (since $n = k + 1$)

subQuestions.questionText:
It is given that the general term of a quadratic number pattern is $T_n = n^2 + bn + 9$ and the first term of the first differences is $7$.

Show that $b = 4$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $3a + b = 7$ (with $a = 1$), so $3 + b = 7$
Mark 2: $b = 4$
(Alternatively $T_2 - T_1 = 7 \Rightarrow (4 + 2b + 9) - (1 + b + 9) = 7 \Rightarrow b = 4$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the value of the $60^{\text{th}}$ term of this number pattern.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution — $T_{60} = (60)^2 + 4(60) + 9$
Mark 2: Answer — $T_{60} = 3\,849$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the general term for the sequence of first differences of the quadratic number pattern. Write your answer in the form $T_p = mp + q$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks — the pattern is $14 \,;\, 21 \,;\, 30 \,;\, 41 \,;\, \ldots$):
Mark 1: First differences $7 \,;\, 9 \,;\, 11 \,;\, \ldots$
Mark 2: Common second difference $2$
Mark 3: Answer — $T_p = 2p + 5$

subQuestions.questionText: Which TWO consecutive terms in the quadratic number pattern have a first difference of $157$?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $157 = 2p + 5$
Mark 2: $p = 76$
Mark 3: The terms are $T_{76}$ and $T_{77}$

subQuestions.questionText:
Sketched is the graph of $h(x) = \dfrac{1}{x + p} + q$. The asymptotes of $h$ intersect at $(1\,;\,2)$.

Write down the values of $p$ and $q$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $p = -1$
Mark 2: $q = 2$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the coordinates of the $x$-intercept of $h$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $\dfrac{1}{x - 1} + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow -2x + 2 = 1 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{1}{2}$
Mark 2: Answer — $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\,;\,0\right)$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the $x$-coordinate of the $x$-intercept of $g$ if $g(x) = h(x + 3)$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $x = \dfrac{1}{2} - 3$
Mark 2: $x = -\dfrac{5}{2}$

subQuestions.questionText: The equation of an axis of symmetry of $h$ is $y = x + t$. Determine the value of $t$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution of $(1\,;\,2)$ — $2 = 1 + t$
Mark 2: $t = 1$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the values of $x$ for which $-2 \leq \dfrac{1}{x - 1}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $\dfrac{1}{x - 1} + 2 \geq 0$
Mark 2: $x \leq \dfrac{1}{2}$
Mark 3: $x > 1$
(i.e. $x \in \left(-\infty\,;\,\dfrac{1}{2}\right]$ or $(1\,;\,\infty)$)

subQuestions.questionText:
The graphs of $f(x) = x^2 - 4x - 5$ and $g(x) = a \cdot 2^x + q$ are sketched.

- E and H are the $x$-intercepts of $f$.
- C is the $y$-intercept of $f$ and lies on the asymptote of $g$.
- The two graphs intersect at D, the turning point of $f$.

Write down the $y$-coordinate of C.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $y = -5$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the coordinates of D.
Determine the values of $a$ and $q$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $q = -5$
Mark 2: Substitution of $(2\,;\,-9)$ — $-9 = a(2)^2 - 5 \Rightarrow -4 = 4a$
Mark 3: $a = -1$, so $g(x) = -2^x - 5$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the range of $g$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $y \in (-\infty\,;\,-5)$ (i.e. $y < -5$, $y \in \mathbb{R}$)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the values of $k$ for which the value of $f(x) - k$ will always be positive.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: The minimum value of $f$ is $-9$
Mark 2: $k < -9$

subQuestions.questionText:
The graphs of $g(x) = 2x + 6$ and $g^{-1}$, the inverse of $g$, are shown in the diagram.

- D and B are the $x$- and $y$-intercepts respectively of $g$.
- C is the $x$-intercept of $g^{-1}$.
- The graphs of $g$ and $g^{-1}$ intersect at A.

Write down the $y$-coordinate of B.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $y = 6$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of $g^{-1}$ in the form $g^{-1}(x) = mx + n$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Swop $x$ and $y$ — $x = 2y + 6$
Mark 2: $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x - 3$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the coordinates of A.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Equating — $\dfrac{1}{2}x - 3 = 2x + 6$
Mark 2: $x = -6$
Mark 3: $y = -6$, so $A(-6\,;\,-6)$
(Alternatively equate $g$ with $y = x$: $2x + 6 = x \Rightarrow x = -6$, $y = -6$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the length of AB.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution — $AB = \sqrt{(6)^2 + (12)^2}$
Mark 2: $AB = \sqrt{180} = 6\sqrt{5} = 13{,}42$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the area of $\triangle ABC$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: $BC = \sqrt{6^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}$
Mark 2: $AB = AC = \sqrt{180}$ (by symmetry of $g$ and $g^{-1}$, midpoint $(3\,;\,3)$)
Mark 3: Perpendicular height $h = \sqrt{(\sqrt{180})^2 - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{72}}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{162} = 9\sqrt{2}$
Mark 4: Substitution — area $\triangle ABC = \dfrac{1}{2} \times BC \times h$
Mark 5: Answer — $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \sqrt{72} \times \sqrt{162} = 54$ units$^2$
(Alternatively $= \dfrac{1}{2}(\sqrt{180})(\sqrt{180})\sin 36{,}86^\circ = 53{,}99$ units$^2$.)

subQuestions.questionText:
$R12\,000$ was invested in a fund that paid interest at $m\%$ p.a., compounded quarterly. After $24$ months, the value of the investment was $R13\,459$.

Determine the value of $m$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $n = 8$ (quarters)
Mark 2: Substitution into the correct formula — $13\,459 = 12\,000\left(1 + \dfrac{m}{400}\right)^8$
Mark 3: $1 + \dfrac{m}{400} = \sqrt[8]{1{,}121\ldots}$
Mark 4: $m = 5{,}78\%$

subQuestions.questionText:
On 31 January 2022, Tino deposited $R1\,000$ in an account that paid interest at $7{,}5\%$ p.a., compounded monthly. He continued depositing $R1\,000$ on the last day of every month. He will make the last deposit on 31 December 2022.

Will Tino have sufficient funds in the account on 1 January 2023 to buy a computer that costs $R13\,000$? Justify your answer by means of an appropriate calculation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $i = \dfrac{0{,}075}{12}$
Mark 2: $n = 12$ (deposits)
Mark 3: $F = \dfrac{1\,000\left[\left(1 + \frac{0{,}075}{12}\right)^{12} - 1\right]}{\frac{0{,}075}{12}} = R12\,421{,}22$
Mark 4: Conclusion — No, he won't be able to buy the computer since $R12\,421{,}22 < R13\,000$ (short by $R578{,}78$)

subQuestions.questionText:
Thabo plans to buy a car that costs $R250\,000$. He will pay a deposit of $15\%$ and take out a loan for the balance. The interest on the loan is $13\%$ p.a., compounded monthly.

Calculate the value of the loan.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: Loan $= 85\% \times R250\,000 = R212\,500$

subQuestions.questionText: The first repayment will be made 6 months after the loan has been granted. The loan will be repaid over a period of 6 years after it has been granted. Calculate the MONTHLY instalment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Grow the loan for 5 months — $A = 212\,500\left(1 + \dfrac{0{,}13}{12}\right)^5$
Mark 2: $A = R224\,262{,}53$
Mark 3: Substitution into the correct formula — $224\,262{,}53 = \dfrac{x\left[1 - \left(1 + \frac{0{,}13}{12}\right)^{-n}\right]}{\frac{0{,}13}{12}}$
Mark 4: $n = 67$ (payments)
Mark 5: Answer — $x = R4\,724{,}96$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine $f'(x)$ from first principles if $f(x) = x^2 + x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution into the formula — $f'(x) = \displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{(x + h)^2 + (x + h) - (x^2 + x)}{h}$
Mark 2: Expansion — $x^2 + 2xh + h^2 + x + h$
Mark 3: Simplification — $\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{2xh + h^2 + h}{h}$
Mark 4: Common factor — $\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{h(2x + h + 1)}{h}$
Mark 5: Answer — $f'(x) = 2x + 1$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine $f'(x)$ if $f(x) = 2x^5 - 3x^4 + 8x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $10x^4$
Mark 2: $-12x^3$
Mark 3: $+8$, so $f'(x) = 10x^4 - 12x^3 + 8$

subQuestions.questionText: The tangent to $g(x) = ax^3 + 3x^2 + bx + c$ has a minimum gradient at the point $(-1\,;\,-7)$. For which values of $x$ will $g$ be concave up?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $g'(x) = 3ax^2 + 6x + b$
Mark 2: $g''(x) = 6ax + 6$
Mark 3: $g''(-1) = 6a(-1) + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow a = 1$
Mark 4: Concave up where $g''(x) > 0 \Rightarrow 6x + 6 > 0 \Rightarrow x > -1$

subQuestions.questionText:
The graph of $y = f'(x) = mx^2 + nx + k$ is drawn. The graph passes through the points $P\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\,;\,0\right)$, $Q(1\,;\,0)$ and $R(0\,;\,1)$.

Determine the values of $m$, $n$ and $k$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (6 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution of $\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\,;\,0\right)$ and $(1\,;\,0)$ — $f'(x) = m\left(x + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)(x - 1)$
Mark 2: Substitution of $(0\,;\,1)$ — $1 = m\left(0 + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)(0 - 1)$
Mark 3: $m = -3$
Mark 4: $f'(x) = -3\left(x^2 - \dfrac{2}{3}x - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = -3x^2 + 2x + 1$
Mark 5: $n = 2$
Mark 6: $k = 1$

subQuestions.questionText:
If it is further given that $f(x) = -x^3 + x^2 + x + 2$:

Determine the coordinates of the turning points of $f$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $x$-coordinates of the turning points — $x = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $x = 1$ (roots of $f'$)
Mark 2: $f\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{49}{27} = 1{,}81$, so $\text{T.P}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\,;\,\dfrac{49}{27}\right)$
Mark 3: $f(1) = 3$, so $\text{T.P}(1\,;\,3)$

subQuestions.questionText: Draw the graph of $f$. Indicate on your graph the coordinates of the turning points and the intercepts with the axes.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: One $x$-intercept — $x = 2$ (from $(x - 2)(-x^2 - x - 1) = 0$, the quadratic factor has no real roots)
Mark 2: Two turning points indicated — $\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\,;\,1{,}81\right)$ and $(1\,;\,3)$
Mark 3: $y$-intercept $(0\,;\,2)$
Mark 4: Shape: negative (decreasing) cubic
Mark 5: All features correctly placed

subQuestions.questionText:
Points E and W are two variable points on $f'$ and are on the same horizontal line.

- $h$ is a tangent to $f'$ at E.
- $g$ is a tangent to $f'$ at W.
- $h$ and $g$ intersect at $D(a\,;\,b)$.

Write down the value of $a$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $a = \dfrac{-\frac{1}{3} + 1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ (the axis of symmetry of the parabola $f'$)
(Alternatively $f''(x) = -6x + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{1}{3}$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the value(s) of $b$ for which $h$ and $g$ will no longer be tangents to $f'$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: The turning point value of $f'$ is $\dfrac{4}{3}$
Mark 2: $b < \dfrac{4}{3}$ units

subQuestions.questionText:
Given $f(x) = x^2$.

Determine the minimum distance between the point $(10\,;\,2)$ and a point on $f$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (8 marks):
Mark 1: Any point on $f$ is $(x\,;\,x^2)$
Mark 2: Substitution — distance $= \sqrt{(x - 10)^2 + (x^2 - 2)^2}$
Mark 3: Simplification — $= \sqrt{x^4 - 3x^2 - 20x + 104}$
Mark 4: Answer (distance expression)
Mark 5: For minimum distance — $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(x^4 - 3x^2 - 20x + 104\big) = 4x^3 - 6x - 20$
Mark 6: Derivative $= 0$ — $(x - 2)(4x^2 + 8x + 10) = 0$ (the quadratic factor has $\Delta = -96$, no real roots)
Mark 7: $x = 2$
Mark 8: Answer — $d = \sqrt{2^4 - 3(2)^2 - 20(2) + 104} = 2\sqrt{17} = 8{,}25$

subQuestions.label: 10.1.1(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
A, B and C are three events. The probabilities of these events (or any combination of them) occurring is given in the Venn diagram. The regions are: A only $= 0{,}05$; A and C only $= 0{,}15$; C only $= 0{,}05$; A and B only $= 0{,}1$; A and B and C $= x$; B and C only $= 0{,}2$; B only $= 0{,}183$; and outside all three events $= y$.

If it is given that the probability that at least one of the events will occur is $0{,}893$, calculate the value of $y$, the probability that none of the events will occur.

subQuestions.label: 10.1.1(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the value of $x$, the probability that all three events will occur.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $x = 0{,}893 - 0{,}733 = 0{,}16$ (subtracting the sum of the known regions)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the probability that at least two of the events will take place.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Values — $P(\text{at least 2 events}) = 0{,}1 + 0{,}15 + 0{,}16 + 0{,}2$
Mark 2: Answer — $= 0{,}61$

subQuestions.questionText: Are events B and C independent? Justify your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: $P(B) = 0{,}643$
Mark 2: $P(C) = 0{,}56$
Mark 3: $P(B \text{ and } C) = 0{,}36$
Mark 4: $P(B) \times P(C) = 0{,}643 \times 0{,}56 = 0{,}36$
Mark 5: Since $P(B \text{ and } C) = P(B) \times P(C)$, events B and C ARE independent

subQuestions.questionText:
A four-digit code is required to open a combination lock. The code must be even-numbered and may not contain the digits $0$ or $1$. Digits may not be repeated.

How many possible 4-digit combinations are there to open the lock?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $4$ (choices for the even last digit, from $\{2\,;\,4\,;\,6\,;\,8\}$)
Mark 2: $7$ (choices for the first of the remaining positions)
Mark 3: $7 \times 6 \times 5 \times 4 = 840$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the probability that you will open the lock at the first attempt if it is given that the code is greater than $5\,000$ and the third digit is $2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks — first digit $> 5$, third digit $= 2$, code even, no repeats):
Mark 1: Start with $5$, $7$ or $9$ — $(3 \times 5 \times 1 \times 3) = 45$
Mark 2: Start with $6$ — $(1 \times 5 \times 1 \times 2) = 10$
Mark 3: Start with $8$ — $(1 \times 5 \times 1 \times 2) = 10$
Mark 4: Total favourable $= 45 + 10 + 10 = 65$
Mark 5: Answer — $P = \dfrac{65}{840} = \dfrac{13}{168} = 0{,}08$
